When Should I See My Dentist About a Moving Implant?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

Noticing that a dental implant feels loose or is moving can be an understandably unsettling experience. Many patients who have invested in implant treatment naturally feel concerned when something doesn't feel quite right, and it's one of the more common reasons people turn to the internet for answers before contacting their dentist.

A moving dental implant is not something to dismiss or monitor indefinitely at home. While some causes are straightforward and manageable, others may require prompt professional attention to protect your long-term oral health and the integrity of the implant itself.

This article aims to provide a calm, balanced overview of why a dental implant may feel loose, what the underlying causes might be, when it is appropriate to seek professional dental advice, and what steps you can take to help maintain your implant's health over the long term. Understanding these factors can help you make informed decisions about your dental care.

A moving dental implant may indicate implant failure, loose components, or peri-implant infection. Early professional assessment is important to identify the cause and explore appropriate treatment options before further complications develop.

What Is a Dental Implant and How Does It Work?

A dental implant is a small titanium post that is surgically placed into the jawbone to act as an artificial tooth root. Over a period of several weeks to months, the implant undergoes a process known as osseointegration, during which the surrounding bone fuses naturally with the titanium surface to create a stable foundation.

Once this integration is complete, a custom-made crown, bridge, or denture is attached to the implant via a component called an abutment. This assembly is designed to function very much like a natural tooth, offering stability, strength, and a natural appearance.

When everything is functioning as intended, a well-placed implant should feel firm and secure — similar to a natural tooth root anchored within the jawbone. Any sensation of movement or instability is a departure from normal, and it is worth understanding what might be causing it.

For those considering implant treatment or seeking to understand the process more fully, our dental implants overview provides detailed information about how implants work and what treatment typically involves.

Common Causes of a Loose or Moving Dental Implant

There are several reasons why a dental implant may feel loose or show signs of movement. These can broadly be categorised into component-related issues and more serious biological concerns.

1. A Loose Abutment or Crown

One of the most common and easily resolved reasons for a moving implant is a loosened abutment screw or a crown that has become detached. The crown or prosthetic tooth sits on top of the implant post and is attached via a small screw. Over time, with the pressures of chewing and normal use, this screw can occasionally work loose.

If you are unsure which component is moving, this explainer on the difference between a loose implant and a loose implant crown can help you prepare for your appointment.

In this scenario, the implant fixture itself remains securely integrated within the bone — it is only the visible component above the gumline that has moved. This is generally straightforward to address during a dental appointment.

2. Peri-Implantitis

Peri-implantitis is a condition involving inflammation and infection of the gum and bone tissue surrounding a dental implant. It shares similarities with gum disease (periodontitis) around natural teeth, but affects the soft and hard tissues around an implant instead.

If left unmanaged, peri-implantitis can lead to progressive bone loss around the implant, which may eventually compromise its stability. This is one of the more significant reasons why a moving implant warrants timely professional evaluation.

3. Incomplete Osseointegration

In some cases, the implant may not have fully integrated with the surrounding bone during the healing phase. This can occur due to a range of factors including certain medical conditions, smoking, poor bone quality, or early loading of the implant before integration is complete. If osseointegration has not been achieved adequately, the implant may remain mobile.

4. Trauma or Excessive Bite Force

An accident involving the mouth or jaw, or persistent excessive bite force (sometimes related to teeth grinding or bruxism), can place undue stress on an implant. Over time, this may affect the bone surrounding the implant or cause structural components to loosen.

Understanding the Science: Why Bone Health Matters for Implant Stability

The long-term success of a dental implant depends substantially on the health and volume of the supporting jawbone. Osseointegration — the biological bonding of the titanium implant surface to surrounding bone tissue — is the cornerstone of implant stability.

Bone is living tissue that remodels continuously throughout life. When a natural tooth or implant is present, the bone receives stimulation through chewing forces, which helps maintain its density and volume. However, if an implant becomes compromised — through infection, insufficient bone support, or ongoing inflammation — the bone can begin to resorb (break down) around the implant site.

Peri-implant bone loss is a key concern because bone, once lost, can be difficult to restore. This is why early intervention matters. Identifying the cause of implant movement at the earliest opportunity gives the treating dentist the best chance of addressing the issue before significant bone loss has occurred.

For additional background, this guide on whether a dental implant can shift or move over time explains related causes and risk factors in more detail.

Conditions such as uncontrolled diabetes, osteoporosis, and long-term use of certain medications can also affect bone density and healing capacity, which is why a thorough medical and dental history is always considered as part of implant assessment and aftercare.

Signs and Symptoms That Warrant a Dental Assessment

Whilst any noticeable movement of a dental implant should prompt a call to your dentist, there are certain accompanying symptoms that make it particularly important to seek an assessment without delay.

You should contact your dentist promptly if you notice any of the following:

  • Visible movement or wobbling of the implant or crown
  • Pain or discomfort around the implant site, particularly when biting or chewing
  • Swelling, redness, or tenderness in the gum tissue surrounding the implant
  • Bleeding from the gum around the implant, particularly if unprovoked
  • A bad taste or unpleasant odour near the implant site
  • Feeling that the bite has changed or that the crown no longer sits correctly
  • Any discharge or signs of infection around the implant

It is worth emphasising that some of these symptoms can have straightforward explanations, and experiencing one or more of them does not necessarily mean the implant has failed. However, they do indicate that a clinical examination is needed so that the cause can be properly assessed and managed.

The general guidance is clear: if your dental implant is moving, contact your dental practice as soon as possible — ideally within 24 to 48 hours of noticing the issue.

Dental implant concerns rarely resolve on their own. In fact, delaying assessment can allow certain problems to progress, particularly where infection or bone loss is involved. The sooner a dentist can examine the implant, take relevant X-rays, and assess the surrounding tissues, the greater the range of options available.

In the meantime, whilst waiting for your appointment:

  • Avoid placing excessive pressure on the implant when chewing
  • Maintain gentle but thorough oral hygiene around the area
  • Do not attempt to adjust or manipulate the implant yourself
  • Avoid very hard or sticky foods near the affected area

If you are experiencing significant pain, swelling, or any signs of spreading infection such as fever, swollen lymph nodes, or difficulty swallowing, seek urgent dental or medical care.

What to Expect at Your Dental Appointment

When you attend for an assessment of a moving implant, your dentist will carry out a thorough clinical examination. This will typically include:

  • A visual and tactile assessment of the implant and surrounding gum tissue
  • Dental X-rays (periapical or cone beam CT in some cases) to evaluate bone levels around the implant
  • Assessment of the implant components to determine whether the movement relates to a loose abutment screw or to the implant fixture itself
  • Review of your medical and dental history, including any changes since the implant was placed

Based on this assessment, your dentist will discuss the findings with you and outline the options available. In many cases, a loose crown or abutment can be re-tightened or replaced relatively simply. More complex situations involving bone loss or infection will require a tailored management plan.

It is important to remember that treatment suitability and outcomes depend on individual clinical circumstances and cannot be predicted in advance. Your dentist will always discuss the most appropriate approach for your specific situation.

Peri-Implantitis: A Closer Look at Infection Around Implants

Peri-implantitis deserves particular attention as it is a significant cause of implant complications in the longer term. It is estimated to affect a meaningful proportion of implant patients to varying degrees, which is why ongoing aftercare and monitoring are emphasised as essential parts of implant treatment.

The condition begins with peri-implant mucositis — inflammation of the soft tissue surrounding the implant without bone loss. At this stage, the condition is generally considered reversible with professional cleaning and improved home care. If left unaddressed, however, it can progress to peri-implantitis, where the underlying bone becomes affected.

Risk factors that may increase susceptibility to peri-implantitis include:

  • A history of periodontitis (gum disease)
  • Smoking
  • Poorly controlled diabetes
  • Insufficient oral hygiene
  • Irregular dental maintenance appointments

This is why patients with dental implants are generally advised to attend regular implant maintenance appointments, during which the implant, surrounding tissues, and bone levels can be carefully monitored. Our implant aftercare and maintenance guidance explains more about how to care for implants and what ongoing monitoring involves.

Prevention and Maintaining Long-Term Implant Health

Whilst not all implant complications can be entirely prevented, there are several practical steps that can help maintain your implant's health and reduce the risk of problems arising.

Daily oral hygiene: Brushing twice daily with a soft-bristle toothbrush, combined with interdental cleaning (using floss, interdental brushes, or a water flosser) around the implant, is essential. Plaque accumulation around implants contributes to inflammation and infection risk.

Regular professional maintenance: Attending scheduled implant maintenance appointments allows your dental team to professionally clean around the implant, assess the gum and bone tissues, and identify any early changes before they progress.

Avoid smoking: Smoking is one of the most significant modifiable risk factors for implant complications, including impaired healing and increased susceptibility to peri-implantitis. Reducing or ceasing smoking supports better implant health outcomes.

Manage teeth grinding (bruxism): If you are aware that you grind your teeth, discuss this with your dentist. A custom nightguard can help protect your implant from the forces associated with bruxism.

Maintain general health: Managing systemic conditions such as diabetes through appropriate medical care can also support better implant health outcomes.

Attend routine dental check-ups: Even if your implant feels fine, regular dental examinations allow your dentist to monitor all aspects of your oral health and catch any early changes.

Key Points to Remember

  • A moving dental implant should always be assessed by a dentist — ideally within 24 to 48 hours of noticing the problem
  • Movement may relate to a loose crown or abutment screw, which is often straightforward to address, or to more complex biological issues such as peri-implantitis or failed osseointegration
  • Symptoms such as pain, swelling, bleeding, or discharge around the implant site warrant prompt professional evaluation
  • Early assessment gives the best opportunity to address any issues before they progress
  • Peri-implantitis is a significant risk factor for implant complications; regular maintenance appointments are an important part of long-term implant care
  • Good oral hygiene, avoiding smoking, and attending regular check-ups all contribute to implant longevity

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a moving dental implant fix itself?

No — a moving dental implant will not resolve without professional intervention. Movement may indicate a loose abutment screw, which is generally straightforward to address, or it may reflect a more significant issue such as bone loss or infection. Neither resolves without assessment and appropriate clinical management. Delaying dental evaluation may allow the underlying cause to progress, potentially limiting the options available. Contact your dental practice as soon as you notice movement.

Is it normal for a dental implant to feel slightly loose shortly after placement?

In the period immediately following implant placement, the implant is in the early stages of osseointegration. During this phase, there should not be visible movement, but some patients may notice minor sensitivity or an unfamiliar sensation. If you are concerned about any movement during or after the healing period, always raise this with your dental team. What is normal will vary between individuals, and your dentist is best placed to reassure you based on a clinical assessment.

How long should a dental implant last?

With appropriate placement, good oral hygiene, and regular professional maintenance, dental implants can last for many years. Individual outcomes vary and depend on numerous factors including bone quality, general health, oral hygiene habits, and lifestyle factors such as smoking. No specific outcome can be guaranteed, as implant longevity is influenced by individual clinical and lifestyle variables. Your dentist can advise on what is realistic for your particular circumstances.

What is the difference between a loose crown and a loose implant?

A loose crown refers to movement of the visible prosthetic tooth or restoration above the gumline, often caused by a loosened abutment screw. The implant fixture in the bone remains stable. A loose implant refers to movement of the implant post itself within the bone, which is a more significant concern. Both warrant dental assessment, but the implications and management differ. A dentist will determine which component is affected through clinical examination and imaging.

Can peri-implantitis be treated?

Yes, peri-implantitis can often be managed, particularly when identified at an early stage. Treatment typically involves professional cleaning around the implant, removal of bacterial deposits from the implant surface, and improvements to home oral hygiene. In more advanced cases, surgical intervention may be discussed to address bone loss. Treatment outcomes depend on the severity of the condition and individual patient factors. Your dentist will assess the situation and outline the most appropriate options for your circumstances.

Will I need to have the implant removed if it is moving?

Not necessarily. The need for implant removal depends on the underlying cause and severity of the problem. In many cases — particularly where the movement relates to a loose component rather than failed osseointegration or significant bone loss — the issue can be resolved without removing the implant. However, in situations where the implant has not integrated successfully or where extensive bone loss has occurred, removal may be the clinically appropriate course of action. This decision is always made on an individual basis following thorough assessment.

Conclusion

A moving dental implant is a signal that professional assessment is needed. Whether the cause is something as straightforward as a loose abutment screw or something that requires more involved management, acting promptly gives you and your dental team the best opportunity to address the situation effectively.

Understanding the potential causes — from loose components and peri-implantitis to incomplete osseointegration — helps patients feel informed and better prepared when attending for an assessment. Maintaining good oral hygiene, attending regular implant maintenance appointments, and seeking advice early when concerns arise are all important aspects of long-term implant care.

If you have noticed that your dental implant feels loose or is moving, do not delay in contacting your dental practice. For those based in London who would like to discuss implant concerns or explore their options, our team offers dental implant consultations tailored to individual needs and circumstances.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.
